passage: In their small town near Nashik, the one bus to the junior college left at 6:40, and Nirmala had missed it twice that week. Each night she meant to sleep by ten and ended up scrolling short videos till one. On Thursday her friend Arohi found her asleep on her desk during the free period. "You look like a ghost," Arohi said. That evening Nirmala left her phone charging in the kitchen next to Aai's tiffin tins, set the old wind-up alarm clock, and wrote her study hours on a card above her bed. The first night she reached for the empty bedside table three times. By Monday she was at the bus stop at 6:30, eating a banana, and Arohi waved from the bus window.

qa.q: What time did the bus to the junior college leave?
qa.a: It left at 6:40.

qa.q: What does Nirmala reaching for the empty table three times suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a restless pull toward the phone; the habit was strong even though she had decided to change.

qa.q: Which of Nirmala's changes made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Charging the phone in the kitchen took the temptation out of the bedroom, so she slept earlier and made the bus.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Nirmala before and after the change?
qa.a: Arohi first worries that Nirmala looks like a ghost, then is glad to see Nirmala at the bus stop on time. 😊

grounding: Shows a teenager replacing late-night scrolling with simple sleep and study habits.

passage: In their village in Mandya, Uma fed the cows before school and did her maths homework on the bus. At lunch her phone buzzed: someone had posted an edited photo of Parul in the class group, her face stuck on a buffalo, with laughing faces piling up underneath. A classmate nudged Uma. "Forward it to the other section." Uma didn't laugh. She typed in the group, "This isn't funny. Delete it," and left. Then she found Parul by the well, eyes red, and walked with her to Headmistress Kamalamma's office. The headmistress looked at the photo, called both classes together that afternoon, and had it deleted in front of her. She rang Parul's mother before the last bell.

qa.q: What had someone stuck Parul's face on in the edited photo?
qa.a: On a buffalo.

qa.q: Why didn't Uma laugh when the classmate nudged her?
qa.a: She felt uncomfortable and sympathetic, knowing the photo would hurt and humiliate Parul.

qa.q: What did Uma do that helped most, and why?
qa.a: Refusing to forward it, speaking up in the group and going with Parul to the headmistress got an adult to stop it the same day.

qa.q: What is it like for Parul when Uma finds her by the well?
qa.a: Parul, already hurt and embarrassed, likely feels less alone with someone walking beside her.

grounding: Shows a teenager balancing chores and study while refusing to share a bullying photo online and taking it to the headmistress.

passage: Anirban's first month as a junior clerk at the block office in Bolpur ended with ₹340 left and three days to go. He sat on the thin mattress in his rented room and opened the notebook he'd started. Rent, paid. Electricity, paid on time at the post office. Mess food, fine. But the column marked "snacks and tea" was longer than he'd expected: small cups, every hour, with anyone who asked. His landlady's daughter Ganga, who kept her mother's shop accounts, looked over his shoulder when she brought the water bill. "The tea's eating you alive," she laughed. That night he drew a line: a flask from his room each morning. Next month, he wrote, the notebook decides, not the tea stall.

qa.q: How much money did Anirban have left with three days to go?
qa.a: He had ₹340 left with three days to go.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel looking at the "snacks and tea" column?
qa.a: He felt surprised and a little embarrassed that small daily cups had added up so much.

qa.q: What choice did Anirban make, and who else could help him plan?
qa.a: He chose to carry a flask each morning; talking his monthly plan over with someone experienced, such as a family member, could help too.

qa.q: How does Ganga see Anirban's accounts?
qa.a: Ganga, used to keeping shop accounts, finds his tea spending funny and points it out in a friendly way.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult in his first job tracking bills and spending on his own and noticing where money leaks away.

passage:
"Gargi, why is everything in the machine pink?"
"Oh no. Is that my red dupatta?"
"Your red dupatta and my white kurta. Former white kurta."
"Hansa, I'm so sorry. At home Ma always sorted everything. I just threw it all in."
"Okay, lesson one: whites separate. Lesson two: read the tag."
"What does the little bucket with a hand mean?"
"Hand wash only. Like your silk top, which is also in there."
"Great. I've ruined two things and I've only been here a week."
"It's fine. Also, the dal is burning."
"The dal!"
Gargi ran, turned off the gas and scraped the pan. "Half is fine."
"Half is dinner. Tomorrow we're making a chore chart."

qa.q: What colour was everything in the machine?
qa.a: Everything was pink.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel after ruining two things in the first week?
qa.a: Gargi felt embarrassed and overwhelmed, realising how much Ma had handled at home.

qa.q: What could Gargi do to get on top of household tasks?
qa.a: Gargi could learn one task at a time from Hansa, like sorting laundry and reading tags, and share the chore chart.

qa.q: What is it like for Hansa to find a pink kurta?
qa.a: Hansa is annoyed about the ruined kurta but stays patient and turns it into a lesson. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young adult in a new flat learning laundry and cooking without a parent to rely on.

passage:
Career cell note, second-year BSc, Tuesday
Ritu came in torn between staying in chemistry and switching to a diploma in food technology. She'd made a two-column list but kept crossing things out. Her friend Sachin, who came with her, said, "She lights up in the canteen kitchen, not in the lab." Ritu laughed but didn't disagree. I asked what she does on free Sundays: she tests pickle recipes and records the acidity. I pointed out that she'd been doing food chemistry for years without calling it that. She sat back and went quiet. We agreed she'll shadow the food-tech lab for a week and talk it over with her parents on Saturday. She left with her list folded in her pocket instead of clutched in her hand.

qa.q: What does Ritu do on free Sundays?
qa.a: She tests pickle recipes and records the acidity.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when she sat back and went quiet?
qa.a: She seemed struck and relieved, seeing that her hobby already pointed to a clear path.

qa.q: What makes the agreed next steps sensible?
qa.a: Shadowing the food-tech lab for a week and talking with her parents lets her test the choice in real life before committing.

qa.q: How does Sachin see Ritu's choice?
qa.a: Sachin has noticed her energy in the canteen kitchen and gently nudges her toward what makes her light up.

grounding: Shows a young adult moving toward committing to a specialised course, observed by a career counsellor.

passage: I'm Karthik, Ojas's roommate. On Saturday he dragged me to the engineering alumni meet in the college auditorium. He'd printed ten copies of his CV and practised a two-line introduction in the mirror. For the first half hour he stood by the snacks table, holding his plate like a shield. Then he walked up to a woman from a water-treatment firm who'd given a talk and asked about a problem she'd mentioned, nothing about jobs. They talked for fifteen minutes. She gave him her card. That night he wrote her a short email thanking her and attaching his project on filters. On Wednesday she replied, offering a call about their summer internship. I don't know what he felt, but he read that email about six times.

qa.q: How many copies of his CV did Ojas print?
qa.a: He printed ten copies.

qa.q: What does Ojas holding his plate like a shield suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt nervous and unsure about approaching strangers at first.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that made the connection work?
qa.a: He asked about her actual work instead of asking for a job, then followed up quickly with thanks and a relevant project.

qa.q: How does Karthik see Ojas's evening?
qa.a: Karthik watches the change from hanging back to making a real contact, and guesses at the excitement from the email being reread.

grounding: Shows a young adult making a first professional contact at an alumni meet and following it up into an internship call.

passage: Thanks for having me, Gurpreet. So, I'm Shalini, final-year electronics, and the idea honestly came from my Nani's kantha quilts. Last winter I was stuck on a project to track posture for people who sit all day. Every sensor we tried was stiff and uncomfortable. At home, watching Nani sew her running stitch, I thought: what if the stitch itself was the circuit? I borrowed conductive thread from the lab, and Nani taught me her patterns. The zigzag ones stretch without breaking; that's the key. We stitched a sensor into a cotton vest, and it notices when your back slumps. My professor laughed at first. Then he asked if Nani would visit the lab. She's coming next Tuesday.

qa.q: What kind of thread did Shalini borrow from the lab?
qa.a: Conductive thread.

qa.q: How did Shalini feel watching Nani stitch?
qa.a: Shalini felt a spark of excitement and curiosity, suddenly seeing the stitch as a possible circuit.

qa.q: What made this idea original?
qa.a: It joined a traditional stitching craft with electronics, solving the stiffness problem with Nani's stretchy zigzag patterns.

qa.q: How did the professor's view of the idea change?
qa.a: The professor laughed at first, then took it seriously enough to invite Nani to the lab.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult combining a grandmother's quilting craft with electronics to create an original project.
